title: Ex-RFK Jr. Aide Accuses White House Insiders of Trading Public Health for Corporate Cash
snippet: Calley Means, a key architect of the 'Make America Healthy Again' movement, claims top Trump administration aides undermined health policies to appease tobacco, pesticide, and pharma lobbyists.
content:
In a explosive series of media appearances, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has publicly accused top White House staff of rampant corruption, alleging that senior officials systematically compromised public health policies to serve corporate interests ahead of the midterm elections.

Speaking on CBS News' Face the Nation and The Joe Rogan Experience podcast, Means targeted former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who resigned late last week, along with key aides James Blair and FDA nominee Dr. Heidi Overton. Means asserted that a entrenched network of former lobbyists inside the administration catered to the tobacco, pharmaceutical, pesticide, and ultra-processed food industries under the guise of raising campaign funds.

Flavored Vapes and High-Stakes Pressure

Central to Means' allegations is a push by White House officials to mandate the approval of fruit-flavored e-cigarettes. According to Means, Wiles and Blair heavily pressured the Food and Drug Administration to clear pathways for flavored vapes to benefit industry donors. Former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned in May, confirmed that he faced relentless pressure from Big Tobacco to approve youth-appealing products, stating he stepped down rather than yield to political corruption.

Blair denied the claims, arguing he was simply tasked by the president to enforce statutory six-month review timelines for nicotine device applications. However, sources familiar with the matter confirmed that corporate lobbyists met directly with administration officials at the president's Florida golf resort to lobby for deregulating e-cigarettes.

Pesticides, Food Reforms, and Supreme Court Battles

Means also pointed to executive actions favoring agrochemical giants like Bayer, the manufacturer of the glyphosate-based herbicide Roundup. Despite longstanding concerns regarding the chemical's carcinogenic risks, an executive order was issued earlier this year to boost domestic glyphosate production. Means accused White House officials of collaborating with the Department of Justice to draft a Supreme Court brief shielding the manufacturer from consumer liability claims.

Furthermore, Means expressed frustration over blocked efforts to establish a official federal definition for ultra-processed foods. He noted that corporate lobbyists actively fought against nutritional transparency to prevent consumers from steering clear of harmful ingredients.

Tensions Over FDA Leadership and Vaccine Approvals

The whistleblower voiced sharp opposition to Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination as the next FDA commissioner, describing her as the primary obstacle to the administration's health reform agenda. Means alleged that Overton weaponized regulatory decisions, pressuring officials to approve Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA, despite Secretary Kennedy's vocal skepticism of mRNA technology.

Despite his harsh criticism of the outgoing staff, Means expressed optimism about incoming Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, claiming Miller remains committed to working alongside Kennedy to enact meaningful, structural reforms aimed at improving American health outcomes.
